name: SQuAD 2.0
summary: 11,873 reading comprehension questions on Wikipedia passages, about half of them unanswerable from the passage, from the SQuAD 2.0 development set with reference answers.
overview:
SQuAD 2.0, the Stanford Question Answering Dataset, tests reading comprehension. Each question comes with a paragraph from a Wikipedia article. When the paragraph answers the question, the answer is a span of its text; otherwise the question is unanswerable, and a system must abstain rather than guess. SQuAD 2.0 was introduced in June 2018. [SQuAD 2.0 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)

The answerable questions come from SQuAD 1.1. Its authors sampled 536 articles from the 10,000 highest-ranked English Wikipedia articles, kept paragraphs of at least 500 characters with images, figures, and tables stripped, and had crowdworkers ask and answer up to five questions per paragraph in their own words, highlighting each answer in the text. For SQuAD 2.0, crowdworkers wrote up to five unanswerable questions per paragraph. Each had to refer to entities in the paragraph and have a plausible answer there, such as a span of the right type, so that it looked like the answerable questions shown beside it. The authors found that these questions were much harder for models of the time than unanswerable questions generated automatically. [SQuAD 1.1 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.05250) and [SQuAD 2.0 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)
methodology:
This snapshot contains all 11,873 questions in dev-v2.0.json at the pinned commit of the SQuAD-explorer repository, which is the file offered for download on the SQuAD website. They cover 1,204 paragraphs from 35 articles: 5,928 answerable questions and 5,945 unanswerable ones. The development set keeps SQuAD 1.1's partition of articles, minus the articles that did not receive unanswerable questions. The test set is hidden; models are scored on it by submission to the maintainers. [Dataset folder](https://github.com/rajpurkar/SQuAD-explorer/tree/eee5fdbf62f8613a7812b03419e6b29617b74fd1/dataset) and [SQuAD 2.0 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)

Each Task Prompt is the upstream question, a line naming the source article by its upstream title, such as Wikipedia article: Sky_(United_Kingdom), and the upstream paragraph. The question and paragraph are verbatim, including leading or trailing spaces on 768 questions and five paragraphs. Twenty-seven Oxygen paragraphs contain line breaks where the article had a subscript, so a formula such as O2 appears as O with 2 on the next line.

For an answerable question, the Solution lists each distinct answer text on its own line, in upstream order. The development set has several crowdworker answers per question, often the same span, and identical texts are listed once; 2,761 questions have one distinct answer and the rest have two to five. Character offsets are not shown. For an unanswerable question, the Solution is Unanswerable followed by the plausible but incorrect answer recorded upstream; 15 unanswerable Oxygen questions have none.

Seven pairs of questions share the same paragraph and question text, so their prompts are identical. In four pairs, two in Steam_engine and two in Economic_inequality, one copy is answerable and the other is marked unanswerable. Two European_Union_law pairs are both answerable with different answer lists, and one Geology pair is unanswerable twice. Each question keeps its own ID.

IDs are the upstream 24-character question IDs, so tasks sort by ID rather than by article. Prompt and solution source links point to the pinned data file without per-question anchors. No task-specific software environment is required. The importer uses only Python's standard library and can be rerun with python3 data/squad-v2/import.py.
scoring:
A system answers each question with a span of text, or with an empty string to abstain. The official evaluation script normalizes answers by lowercasing them and removing punctuation, the articles a, an, and the, and extra whitespace. It then scores each prediction by exact match and by token-overlap F1 against every gold answer and keeps the best. For an unanswerable question the only gold answer is the empty string, so abstaining scores 1 and any other answer scores 0. The reported scores are the average exact match and F1 over all questions, with separate figures for answerable and unanswerable questions. If a file of predicted no-answer probabilities is supplied, the script also reports the best scores over abstention thresholds. [Evaluation script](https://github.com/rajpurkar/SQuAD-explorer/blob/eee5fdbf62f8613a7812b03419e6b29617b74fd1/evaluate-v2.0.py) and [SQuAD 2.0 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)

To estimate human performance, the authors had more crowdworkers answer every development and test question, collecting 4.8 answers per question on average, and took a majority vote. Humans scored 86.3 exact match and 89.0 F1 on the development set. The strongest model in the paper scored 65.1 and 67.6, and a system that always abstains scores 48.9 F1 on the test set. [SQuAD 2.0 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)

Compare results on the same split; development and hidden-test scores are reported separately on the SQuAD leaderboard. Benchopedia's sweep uses the official normalized exact match for its solve verdict, including explicit abstention. The official token F1 metric is available through the evaluation script in How to run. [SQuAD website](https://rajpurkar.github.io/SQuAD-explorer/)
limitations:
Every answer is a span of a single paragraph, so the benchmark does not test answering from several documents, writing free-form answers, or finding the relevant passage. The SQuAD 2.0 authors note that models did well on SQuAD 1.1 by learning context and type-matching heuristics, and that this success did not ensure robustness to distracting sentences. An unanswerable question only lacks an answer in its paragraph; elsewhere in Wikipedia it may have one. [SQuAD 1.1 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.05250) and [SQuAD 2.0 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)

The labels are crowdsourced. In a manual check of 100 unanswerable development questions, the authors judged 93% to be truly unanswerable, and four pairs of identical prompts carry conflicting labels. Exact match and F1 reward the specific spans annotators chose, so a correct answer worded differently, or a model that writes a sentence instead of a span, can score poorly. The development set has been public since 2018 and is drawn from Wikipedia, so a score alone cannot establish that a model was tested on unseen material. [SQuAD 2.0 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03822)
